body.html: Stop bleeding in steps: direct pressure, then wound packing, then a tourniquet for massive limb bleeding. A victim who loses more than 25% of their blood volume may develop shock. As always: Check, Call, Care.

The severity of the injury sets the rate of loss. Ask where the bleeding is (think of internal as well as external), whether it is arterial or venous, and whether more than 25% of blood volume may be lost. Check carefully for profuse bleeding, feeling inside bulky clothing and underneath the patient.
Protect yourself (gloves), call the EMS, then apply a dressing and press. For deep wounds, pack the wound with gauze to press directly on the bleeding source.

Indicated for massive, life-threatening limb bleeding, ideally by a trained person, and only when direct pressure fails. It is a band so tight that all distal flow stops. Rescue teams should carry commercial models such as the CAT (Combat Application Tourniquet) or SOFT; improvised ones can be made from clothing, towels or tent material.

How: wide, flat, non-stretch band 7.5 to 10 cm (never wire or rope); wrap several times as close above the wound as possible; overhand knot, stick on the knot, second knot; twist until bleeding stops; tie or tape the stick; note the time. More than an hour from care: loosen very slowly at 60 minutes while pressing the wound; retighten if heavy bleeding returns; if manageable, leave it loose in place.

For pelvic trauma: remove belts and pocket items; slide the improvised material under the buttocks and centre it on the greater trochanters; cross it over the front of the pelvis, pull both ends and secure with a knot, clamp or duct tape.

Sudden cardiac arrest is the sudden cessation of organised cardiac activity with haemodynamic collapse, most often from ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia, occasionally pulseless electrical activity (PEA) or asystole. Survival depends on the chain of survival and on starting basic life support on time.

Sudden cardiac death is 15 to 20% of overall mortality in industrialised nations and about 50% of cardiovascular deaths, and is the first manifestation of heart disease in up to half of cases. Coronary artery disease dominates in older people; channelopathies and cardiomyopathies in people 35 and under; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and anomalous coronary origin in young athletes. Non-cardiac causes: trauma, toxins, respiratory distress.

Check responsiveness: tap the shoulders and shout. Call the EMS (15) immediately. Open the airway and look for absent or abnormal breathing: agonal gasping is a sign of arrest, and a brief seizure-like episode can occur at onset. Health professionals check a pulse for no more than 10 seconds. If unresponsive with abnormal breathing, or in any doubt, assume cardiac arrest and start CPR; the call-taker can guide you.

Compressions: lower half of the sternum, depth 5 to 6 cm, rate 100 to 120/min, full recoil, no leaning, as few interruptions as possible, on a firm surface. Ventilation if trained: 30 compressions : 2 breaths, by mouth-to-mouth, mouth-to-mask, bag-valve-mask (high oxygen) or an improvised glove barrier; if unable or unwilling, give continuous compressions.

Attach the AED as soon as it arrives: right pad below the right clavicle, above the nipple; left pad on the left side below the armpit over the lower ribs. Pads must not touch; dry the chest and remove clothing; follow the voice prompts. Shockable rhythms (VF, pulseless VT): shock, then CPR for 2 minutes. Non-shockable (asystole, PEA): CPR for 2 minutes, then reassess. The lecture closes with paediatric cardiac arrest algorithms.

Shock is widespread failure of the circulation to oxygenate and nourish the body: a transition between life and death. At cell level it disturbs mitochondrial energy transfer and leads to toxic metabolites. Four families: cardiogenic, hypovolaemic, distributive, obstructive.

Two systems in series: the macrocirculation generates oxygenated flow; the microcirculation distributes it to tissues. Arteries are resistive, veins capacitive; exchange occurs in capillaries. MAP = CO × SVR and CO = SV × HR; stroke volume depends on preload, contractility and afterload; the ejected volume and the arterial tree together create perfusion pressure (ventriculo-arterial coupling).

Oxygen delivery: TaO2 = CaO2 × CO, with CaO2 = 1.34 × Hb × SaO2. Fick: VO2 = CO × (CaO2 - CvO2). Cellular hypoperfusion shifts metabolism to anaerobic pathways: lactate accumulates, causing metabolic acidosis. The baroreflex responds to falling pressure with more sympathetic and less parasympathetic activity.

Peripheral hypoperfusion: mottling, cold, pale or cyanotic extremities, capillary refill over 3 seconds. Reduced regional flow: altered consciousness (confusion, agitation, coma), oliguria, tachypnoea, tachycardia.

Cardiogenic: reduced contractility (MI, myocarditis, drug intoxication), rhythm disorders (high-degree AV block, SVT), mechanical causes (acute mitral or aortic regurgitation, intracavitary thrombus, septal rupture). Hypovolaemic: haemorrhage, GI losses, extensive burns, dehydration; in haemorrhage, anaemia also cuts oxygen transport. Distributive: septic, anaphylactic, inflammatory (pancreatitis, burns), spinal shock; vasodilation and capillary leak cause relative hypovolaemia and poor oxygen extraction. Obstructive: cardiac tamponade, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax.

Haemodynamic assessment: non-invasive and invasive arterial pressure, central venous pressure, pulmonary artery catheter (Swan-Ganz), cardiac output by the Fick principle, echocardiography for stroke volume, and blood gases (arterial lactate, venous oxygen saturation).

Management: symptomatic treatment to restore oxygen delivery (oxygen, fluid filling, catecholamines: adrenaline, noradrenaline, dobutamine) plus etiological treatment of the cause.

The GI tract's jobs are motility, secretion, digestion, absorption, storage, endocrine signalling, protection and expulsion, with thirst and hunger as behavioural regulators. Three emergencies converge on systemic inflammation, capillary leak, coagulopathy and multi-organ failure: acute liver failure, acute mesenteric ischaemia and acute pancreatitis. The opening case: a patient starting antituberculosis treatment develops jaundice, encephalopathy and GI bleeding from drug-induced acute liver failure.

The liver (2 lobes, 8 segments, about 1,000 lobules) receives 25% of cardiac output: the portal vein gives 75% of flow but only 50% of oxygen; the hepatic artery gives 25% of flow and 50% of oxygen. Thirst responds to high plasma osmolality (hypothalamic osmoreceptors) or low pressure (baroreceptors); losses include urine, faeces, sweat and insensible losses. Liver metabolic functions: glucose and glycogen, cholesterol and proteins, fat/protein/carbohydrate metabolism, drug metabolism (cytochrome P450), detoxification, bile, acute-phase proteins, haemoglobin processing and iron storage, clotting factors, blood reservoir. Ammonia from protein breakdown is converted to urea.

Liver panel: damage (ALT, AST, AST/ALT ratio, GLDH), biliary disease (GGT, ALP, bilirubin), synthesis (albumin, cholinesterase, prothrombin time). The true tests of liver function are PT and albumin; enzymes only show injury. Pancreatitis: amylase rises in 2 to 12 h, peaks at 24 h, normalises in 3 to 5 days, and is non-specific (salivary disease, renal failure, gynaecological disease, ischaemia; may be normal in hypertriglyceridaemia); lipase rises in 4 to 8 h, peaks at 24 h, stays up 8 to 14 days and is more sensitive and specific. Endoscopy: upper (dyspepsia, GERD with alarm signs, dysphagia, upper bleeding, anaemia, vomiting) and lower (lower bleeding, bowel habit change, IBD, imaging abnormalities). Imaging: ultrasound (liver, gallstones), CT (obstruction, ischaemia, trauma), MRCP (choledocholithiasis), endoscopic ultrasound (pancreatic cancer, biliary strictures).

Drug-induced acute liver failure: antibiotics, paracetamol (the commonest cause), NSAIDs, antiepileptics, antituberculosis drugs, herbs and supplements. Mechanisms: toxic metabolites, immune attack on drug-P450 adducts, apoptosis via TNF receptors, mitochondrial dysfunction (low ATP, lactate, ROS, steatosis), bile-duct injury and cholestasis. Brain oedema follows hyperammonaemia (astrocyte glutamine), inflammation and a leaky BBB.

Acute mesenteric ischaemia: sudden hypoperfusion of the small bowel and right colon from occlusive or non-occlusive arterial or venous obstruction; pain out of proportion to examination, progressing to necrosis, peritonitis and sepsis; watershed areas are Griffiths' and Sudeck's points; CT angiography is the first imaging.

Acute pancreatitis: activation of digestive enzymes inside the gland; 80% from gallstones or alcohol (gallstones slightly commoner); a stone at the ampulla obstructs the duct, enzymes activate, autodigestion leads to SIRS and multi-organ failure.

Supportive: oxygen, IV fluids, vasopressors, correct electrolytes, acid-base and coagulation. Specific: remove the offending drug; N-acetylcysteine for paracetamol toxicity with any liver injury; liver transplantation. Mesenteric ischaemia: restore flow fast (endovascular if no necrosis), resect necrotic bowel, preserve length, limit reperfusion injury; infarction carries a poor prognosis. Pancreatitis with biliary obstruction: ERCP.

The endocrine system coordinates cell and organ function to maintain homeostasis: sodium, water and blood pressure; calcium and phosphate; energy balance and fuel use; the stress response; reproduction, growth and senescence. The hypothalamus leads it through the pituitary. Its dysregulation produces multisystem emergencies: adrenal crisis, diabetic ketoacidosis and thyroid storm.

The adrenal cortex has three layers: zona glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), reticularis (androgens: DHEA, androstenedione); the medulla makes catecholamines for the stress response. Insufficiency is primary (gland destruction; Addison disease appears when about 90% of function is lost, so both cortisol and aldosterone fail) or secondary (low ACTH, commonly after prolonged glucocorticoid therapy).

Chronic causes: chronic steroid use, HIV, tuberculosis, autoimmune adrenalitis, congenital disorders, infiltration (sarcoidosis, haemochromatosis, amyloidosis), cancer, surgery or irradiation. Acute causes: drugs (steroid withdrawal, etomidate, ketoconazole), sepsis, adrenal or pituitary haemorrhage, Sheehan syndrome, trauma. Presentation: nonspecific weakness, weight loss, abdominal pain, fever; classically refractory hypotension, often mimicking septic shock, sometimes without reflex tachycardia; think of it in anyone on more than 7.5 mg prednisone for over 3 weeks. Labs: hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia. Management: ABCs, saline bolus, rule out sepsis, antibiotics if needed, vasopressors, send cortisol and ACTH, then hydrocortisone.

Islets: alpha cells → glucagon (raises glucose), beta cells → insulin (lowers glucose), delta cells → somatostatin (inhibits both). Insulin increases glucose entry and glycogen synthesis, inhibits glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis (hormone-sensitive lipase) and fatty-acid oxidation. Glucagon does the reverse and increases beta-oxidation.

DKA: without insulin, cells starve despite hyperglycaemia; fatty acids make ketones → ketoacidosis; glucose in the urine causes osmotic diuresis and dehydration; acidosis shifts K+ out of cells (serum hyperkalaemia) while total body potassium is depleted. Signs: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, abdominal pain, vomiting, confusion, Kussmaul breathing with a fruity odour; critical cases: profound hypotension, coma. Treatment: IV insulin, water and salt, correct electrolytes, avoid hypokalaemia, close monitoring, prevent cerebral oedema.

Thyroid hormone drives growth and development (bone, brain), ventilation, cardiac output, renal function and metabolism (appetite, lipolysis, heat production). Thyrotoxicosis is hypermetabolism from excess hormone (Graves disease, Hashimoto thyroiditis, De Quervain thyroiditis, secreting tumours). Precipitants of storm: infection, surgery, acute coronary syndrome, stroke, neck trauma, stopping medication, hormone ingestion, iodinated contrast.

Presentation: tachycardia often over 140/min, fever sometimes over 41 °C, sweating, GI symptoms, agitation or delirium; critical: high-output heart failure, AF with rapid response, coma, seizures. Management: ABCs, fluids, control agitation, aggressive cooling, treat the precipitant, beta-blockade, block synthesis (propylthiouracil, methimazole), block T4 → T3 (dexamethasone), block release (iodine).

The immune system recognises danger, eliminates threats, repairs tissues and tolerates self. It works through two intertwined arms, innate and adaptive. Its dysregulation causes immunodeficiency, hypersensitivity, autoimmunity or failed tumour surveillance; its knowledge gave vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, checkpoint inhibitors and transplant tolerance.

The first line of defence, also clearing damaged cells. Two main reactions: inflammation (leukocytes and plasma proteins against mainly extracellular microbes) and antiviral defence (NK cells kill infected cells; type I interferons block viral replication). Defence at every stage: epithelia and mucus at portals of entry; resident macrophages, dendritic cells and mast cells in tissues that release cytokines; complement in the blood. Recognition uses pattern recognition receptors for PAMPs and DAMPs, on the cell surface, in endosomes and in the cytosol. Phagocytes (neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages) are recruited, ingest and kill microbes. Innate reactions provide the second signal needed to activate lymphocytes.

Adaptive responses need antigen stimulation, proliferation and differentiation, so they take several days. Humoral immunity (B lymphocytes, antibodies) and cellular immunity (T lymphocytes); secondary responses are faster and stronger thanks to memory. Homeostasis: macrophages silently engulf dead cells and release IL-10 and TGF-β (tolerance, repair); dendritic cells induce self-tolerance without danger signals; NK cells kill cells lacking MHC I (perforin, granzyme); complement C3b opsonises.

Primary immunodeficiencies: genetic, from birth; recurrent, severe or opportunistic infections, growth delay, autoimmunity. IgA deficiency (commonest; ENT and GI infections, often silent) and SCID (no T or B cells; emergency, bone marrow transplant). Treated by immunoglobulin replacement, transplant, gene therapy, prophylaxis. Secondary: HIV (CD4 loss), chemotherapy, long-term steroids, immunosuppressants, diabetes, renal or liver failure, blood cancers; reactivation of TB or herpes; cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in HIV.

Allergy: hypersensitivity through immune mechanisms; atopy is the tendency to make IgE. Type I: sensitisation makes IgE, re-exposure degranulates mast cells and basophils (histamine, leukotrienes) within minutes. Anaphylaxis: skin, respiratory, GI, cardiovascular and neurological signs; treat with intramuscular adrenaline in the thigh without delay, supine with legs raised, oxygen, fluids, antihistamines, corticosteroids, hospital monitoring. Autoimmunity: loss of tolerance, autoantibodies or self-reactive T cells: SLE (anti-DNA, multisystem), multiple sclerosis (T-cell demyelination); immunosuppressants and biologics (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6).

Tumour surveillance: NK cells (absent MHC I), CD8+ CTLs (tumour antigens on MHC I), CD4+ Th1 cells, M1 macrophages and dendritic cells. Escape: loss of MHC I, inhibitory molecules, immunosuppressive cytokines, regulatory T cells and M2 macrophages, T-cell anergy or exhaustion; hence immunotherapies (checkpoint antibodies, vaccines, engineered T cells).

Vaccination: controlled exposure to antigen (inactivated or attenuated microbe, protein, RNA) that creates B and T memory; boosters when immunity wanes or the pathogen changes (influenza). Rejection: hyperacute (minutes to hours, preformed antibodies, thrombosis), acute (days to weeks, T cells against donor MHC), chronic (months to years, fibrosis). Immunosuppressants: corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors (ciclosporin, tacrolimus), antiproliferatives (azathioprine, mycophenolate), antibodies (anti-IL-2R, anti-CD3); risks: opportunistic infections, lymphoma and skin cancers, organ toxicity.

The skull is a rigid box holding brain, CSF and blood. Normal intracranial pressure (ICP) in adults is 5 to 15 mmHg; raised ICP is 20 mmHg or more. When ICP rises, cerebral perfusion falls, ischaemia causes more swelling, and ICP rises further.

ICP rises transiently with movement and position, pain, fever, coughing and straining. Monro-Kellie doctrine: the cranium is a fixed volume; an increase in brain, blood or CSF raises ICP, and the only way to lower ICP is to decrease one of them; every treatment works on this principle.

The brain is 2 to 3% of body mass but receives about 20% of the circulating blood. CPP = MAP - ICP. Cerebral blood flow is autoregulated for CPP between 60 and 160 mmHg; below 60, ischaemia; above 160, hypertensive encephalopathy. CBF also depends on PaO2 and PaCO2. The blood-brain barrier selectively controls exchanges; its dysfunction underlies cerebral oedema, a major cause of raised ICP.

The ICP waveform has a baseline plus small, fast cardiac pulsations and larger, slower respiratory waves; both are needed to describe ICP. The pressure-volume curve is flat at first (compensation) then steep. Cerebral oedema types: vasogenic (BBB breakdown, e.g. tumours), cytotoxic (cell swelling), interstitial (hydrocephalus) and osmotic. Causes include masses and haematomas, oedema and hydrocephalus (enlarged ventricles, effaced sulci).

Treatments target brain, blood or CSF volume. Steroids help vasogenic oedema (tumours): they reduce CSF production and restore membrane permeability. Glucose control avoids cellular oedema. Hypothermia lowers CBF, ICP and metabolism. Skull trephination (burr hole) can save a patient with an acute epidural haematoma and deteriorating signs (falling consciousness, anisocoria, hemiparesis). Surgery is definitive for space-occupying lesions: craniotomy or ventriculostomy with drainage; shunts for hydrocephalus.

First aid is the immediate care given to an injured or suddenly ill person before professional help arrives. Its three aims: preserve life, prevent worsening, promote recovery. It applies to medical emergencies (chest pain, tachycardia, acute dyspnoea, altered mental status), trauma, environmental conditions, respiratory problems, intoxications and envenomations.

title: The first responder and the scene
subject: subj:firstaid

body.html:
A first responder can be a professional, a trained person or a layperson. The role: stay calm, act within your training, call for professional help, and secure the scene before acting. Priorities: emotional self-control, then the safety of yourself, your team and the victim. Do not rush in; eliminate physical dangers; do not assume you know how injured the victim is; protect yourself from blood and body fluids with PPE.

Hazards: biohazards and chemicals, fire and fumes, electricity, water, traffic, falling objects and unstable structures, slippery surfaces, sharp edges and glass, explosives, confined spaces, heights, and aggressive people.

Road accident: switch off all ignitions, move casualties to safety, immobilise an upright vehicle (hand brake, blocks under the wheels), never try to right a vehicle on its side, stabilise it only if safe and trained.

title: The three Cs and the primary survey
subject: subj:firstaid

body.html:
Once the scene is safe: Check the victim, Call the EMS, Care for the victim. The check is the primary survey (ABCDE): Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability (neurological status including neck injury), Exposure/Environment. Call early and give an exact location (map, phone, GPS, landmarks); the Moroccan emergency number taught is 15.

A: is the airway open? After a fall or major trauma, suspect the cervical spine and apply spinal motion restriction; do not move the person unless unsafe. B: look, listen, feel for normal breathing for at most 10 seconds; listen for wheeze or stridor; look for swelling, choking and cyanosis; use pulse oximetry if available.

In a supine unresponsive victim the tongue can fall back and block the airway. Open it with a head tilt and chin lift (hand on forehead, fingertips under the chin) or a jaw thrust (modified jaw thrust in trauma); an improvised nasopharyngeal airway can help. Clear blood, vomit, loose dentures and debris with a two-finger sweep without pushing them deeper. If breathing adequately, turn the victim into the recovery position (arm bent or straight; prone variant; left side in pregnancy) and keep checking breathing until EMS arrives.

Obstruction of the upper airway above the vocal cords by the tongue, broken teeth, dentures or food. Partial: the victim can speak or cough forcefully; encourage coughing and monitor. Complete: no speech, no air exchange, no cough; the universal choking sign (hands at the neck); untreated it leads to hypoxic cardiac arrest.

Care: sweep visible material, remove loose dentures; give 2 to 4 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades (victim bent forward); then the Heimlich manoeuvre: from behind, fist in the upper abdomen just below the ribs, 2 to 3 sudden firm squeezes. Small child: face down or upside down. Infant: face down on the forearm, head lower, 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts. Obese or pregnant: chest thrusts on the breastbone instead of the abdomen. A lying victim can also receive thrusts.

The kidneys regulate extracellular volume by adjusting NaCl and water excretion. Acute kidney injury (AKI) is an abrupt loss of kidney function that causes life-threatening disturbances of volume, electrolytes and acid-base balance. Three frameworks: prerenal, intrinsic, postrenal.

Renal blood flow is 20% of cardiac output. The glomerular capillary is the only bed flanked by two resistance vessels (afferent and efferent arterioles), whose tone sets glomerular pressure. Functions: filtration, reabsorption, secretion, excretion; blood pressure regulation; hormones (erythropoietin, active vitamin D, renin).

GFR = Pnet × area; glomerular hydraulic pressure about 60 mmHg favours filtration, opposed by Bowman's hydrostatic pressure and capillary oncotic pressure. Normal GFR is about 120 (women) and 130 (men) mL/min/1.73 m², about 180 L/day, falling about 1 mL/min/year after 40; estimated with creatinine clearance.

The juxtaglomerular apparatus autoregulates renal blood flow and GFR for perfusion pressures of 80 to 180 mmHg: low perfusion or low NaCl at the macula densa (NKCC2) makes granular cells release renin. About 99% of filtered water is reabsorbed: passively in the proximal tubule and loop, and via ADH in the collecting duct, which sets final concentration.

Prerenal (commonest, 40 to 55%): true hypovolaemia (haemorrhage, GI and renal losses, third spacing) or low effective arterial volume (cardiogenic or septic shock, cirrhosis, hypoalbuminaemia, anaphylaxis); reverses quickly if perfusion is restored, but prolonged ischaemia leads to ATN.

Intrinsic: ischaemic and septic acute tubular necrosis (commonest), allergic interstitial nephritis, nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, contrast), endogenous toxins (haemoglobin, myoglobin, bilirubin, urate in tumour lysis), large-vessel (thrombosis, embolism) and small-vessel disease (atheroembolism, HUS, malignant hypertension, rejection, vasculitis).

Postrenal: obstruction of both ureters (or one in a solitary kidney), bladder outlet (commonest: prostate, anticholinergics, neurogenic bladder) or urethra; relief usually restores GFR if not prolonged. AKI also injures distant organs (lung, heart, brain, liver, gut, immunity).

Often asymptomatic early; later vomiting and diarrhoea, thirst and cramps, oedema, flank pain (obstruction), reduced urine. Look for exposure to nephrotoxins, trauma, sepsis and hypotension. Signs of hypovolaemia (tachycardia, hypotension, dry mucosa, poor turgor) or hypervolaemia (oedema, weight gain), confusion, asterixis, livedo reticularis (atheroembolism), rash (allergy).

Management: correct reversible causes (fluids for prerenal; catheter, nephrostomy or stent for postrenal; stop culprit drugs, immunosuppression for glomerulonephritis), avoid further injury, correct fluids and electrolytes; no drug directly treats AKI. Diuretics only for fluid overload, targeting 0.5 to 1 mL/kg/h. Dialysis for refractory overload, uraemic pericarditis, severe electrolyte or acid-base disorders. Complications: pulmonary oedema, hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia, metabolic acidosis, uraemia, progression to CKD, cardiovascular events; urine under 400 mL/day worsens prognosis. Prevent by limiting nephrotoxins in high-risk patients and maintaining perfusion.

Trauma and burns are among the commonest causes of preventable death and disability. The first minutes are decisive. Common trauma causes: road accidents, falls, assaults, sports injuries. Goals: preserve life, limit damage and complications, and ensure safe transfer.

ABCDE: Airway with cervical spine stabilisation, Breathing, Circulation with control of external haemorrhage, Disability (neurological status), Exposure (undress completely but prevent hypothermia). Circulation: pulses first, skin colour; a palpable pulse suggests a minimum systolic pressure of about radial 80, femoral 70, carotid 60 mmHg. Major haemorrhage hides in five places: chest, abdomen, retroperitoneum, thigh, and the outside.

Suspect a cervical injury after a fall or dive from height, crushing, road or sports accidents. If awake, let the person hold their neck in a comfortable position; never force someone into a position. In an unresponsive supine victim, kneel behind the head and hold it in line (head or trapezius squeeze). Tools: horse collar made from a blanket, cervical extrication splints, long spine boards with padding.

Splinting: expose the limb, check neurovascular status before and after, cover open wounds with dry sterile dressings, immobilise the joint above and below the fracture, cool and elevate, reassess often. Pelvic splint for pelvic injuries.

Helmets: motorcycle and motorsport helmets should be removed pre-hospital (they hinder airway care and flex the neck). Absolute contraindications: neck pain or paraesthesia during removal, or an impaled object. Technique: rescuer 1 holds in-line from above (fingers on the mandible); rescuer 2 cuts the strap and takes over stabilisation (hand on the mandible angle, other on the occiput); rescuer 1 spreads the helmet over the ears, removes glasses, and tilts it back over the nose.

Control bleeding first. Keep the part cold but not frozen: wrap it in a sterile or clean cloth moistened with saline or water, place it in a sealed bag, then put that bag in another bag of ice or ice water (or with cold packs).

Stop the burning: remove the source; roll a burning victim or wrap them in a blanket; remove hot clothing, jewellery and debris. Chemical burns: rinse with large amounts of water for at least 10 minutes; never use a neutralising agent (it generates heat). Hydrofluoric acid: irrigate, then topical calcium gluconate gel. Eyes: irrigate copiously. Phosphorus: keep covered with water (it ignites in air; UV light shows embedded particles).

Then a primary survey and cooling with water for about 30 minutes. Burns under 10% of body surface can be cooled longer for pain; prolonged cooling of large burns risks hypothermia and skin maceration; cooling started more than 30 minutes after the burn only helps pain. Remove rings from burned fingers and toes to avoid a tourniquet effect.
